content: Always inform your healthcare provider about all prescription and over-the-counter (OTC) medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, and other supplements you are currently using. Dexlansoprazole can influence the absorption of certain other medications. Ensure you provide your healthcare provider with a complete list of all medications you are taking or have recently taken, as this may not be an exhaustive list of potential interactions with dexlansoprazole. If you or someone else has accidentally taken too much dexlansoprazole, seek immediate medical attention. Call 911 or contact a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. If you miss a dose of dexlansoprazole, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and only take the next scheduled dose. Do not take double or extra doses to make up for the missed one. Dexlansoprazole is used to treat heartburn and other conditions caused by excessive stomach acid, such as gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and erosive esophagitis (EE). It may also be prescribed for other conditions as determined by your healthcare provider. The medication works by reducing the amount of acid produced by the stomach. Dexlansoprazole is available as delayed-release oral capsules in 30 mg and 60 mg doses. It should be stored at room temperature, between 68°F to 77°F (20°C to 25°C), and can tolerate short-term exposure to temperatures between 59°F to 86°F (15°C to 30°C), such as during transportation. The most common side effects of dexlansoprazole include diarrhea, stomach pain, nausea, symptoms of the common cold, vomiting, gas, headache (in children aged 12 to 17 years), and sore throat (in children aged 12 to 17 years). If any of these side effects bother you, inform your healthcare provider. There may be other side effects not listed here, so contact your healthcare provider if you suspect you are experiencing a side effect. Serious side effects of dexlansoprazole, though less common, include: 1. Kidney problems: Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis can occur at any time during treatment. If you notice a decrease in urine output or blood in your urine, contact your doctor immediately. 2. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea: Overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) in the gut can occur. Symptoms include watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea, blood in stool, severe stomach cramps, and fever. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if these symptoms occur. 3. Severe skin reactions: Conditions such as Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) can occur and may be life-threatening. If you develop a rash, stop taking dexlansoprazole and contact your healthcare provider immediately. Seek emergency help if you experience painful red or purple skin that peels, flat red rashes or blisters on the skin, mouth, nose, or genitals, or red, painful, watery eyes. 4. Severe allergic reaction (DRESS): Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS) can affect multiple organs, including the liver, kidneys, and heart. Symptoms include skin rash, hives, fever, swollen lymph nodes, shortness of breath, swelling in the feet or legs, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). Stop using the medication and seek immediate medical attention if these symptoms occur. 5. Lupus: Dexlansoprazole can cause or worsen lupus, an autoimmune disorder. Notify your provider if you experience new or worsening joint pain or a rash on your arms or cheeks. 6. Vitamin B-12 deficiency: Long-term use (3 years or more) of dexlansoprazole can reduce vitamin B-12 absorption, leading to deficiency. Symptoms include a sore tongue, weakness, or tingling/numbness in the hands or feet. Contact your healthcare provider if these occur. 7. Hypomagnesemia: Prolonged use of dexlansoprazole can lead to low magnesium levels, which may cause seizures, heart rhythm problems, dizziness, muscle spasms, or changes in heart rate. Stop using the medication and contact your healthcare provider if these symptoms occur. 8. Bone loss and fractures: Long-term or high-dose use of dexlansoprazole may increase the risk of bone loss and fractures, particularly in older adults. 9. Severe allergic reactions: Symptoms include difficulty breathing, wheezing, rapid heartbeat, fever, swollen lymph nodes, swelling of the face, lips, mouth, tongue, or throat, trouble swallowing, itching, rash, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or fainting. Stop using the medication and seek immediate medical attention if these occur. Dexlansoprazole should not be used by individuals allergic to its ingredients, other proton pump inhibitors, or specific components of the product. Always consult your pharmacist for a complete list of ingredients. Before taking dexlansoprazole, inform your healthcare provider about all prescription and OTC medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, and supplements you are using. Certain medications, such as methotrexate, digoxin, warfarin, tacrolimus, antiretroviral drugs, St. John’s Wort, and rifampin, may interact with dexlansoprazole. Discuss these with your provider to avoid potential interactions. Dexlansoprazole is not recommended for immediate relief of heartburn, as it may take 1 to 4 days to take full effect. It should only be used as prescribed by a healthcare provider and not shared with others, even if they have similar symptoms. Keep it out of reach of children and do not chew, cut, or crush the capsules. If swallowing is difficult, the capsule contents can be sprinkled on one tablespoon of applesauce and swallowed immediately without mixing with other foods. The safety of dexlansoprazole during pregnancy or breastfeeding is not well established. Inform your healthcare provider if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Dexlansoprazole does not have known interactions with food or drinks, but it is unclear if alcohol consumption affects the medication. Always consult your healthcare provider for guidance.
